\chapter{When the Words Run Out --- Help, a Moment, Again, I Don't Know, What Does It Mean}
\label{ch:reparaciones}
\hlchaptermodality{303}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for help, ask for a moment, ask for another go, admit I do not know, and ask what a word means in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C303-que-significa: repair a stalled exchange five ways, ending with the question that earns a meaning.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la ayuda]{la ayuda — the word that stands beside you}

\label{lesson:ES-C303-ayuda}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la ayuda} — \textquotedblleft{}help.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{adiutare} was built from \emph{iuvare}, \textquotedblleft{}to give strength,\textquotedblright{} with \emph{ad-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward.\textquotedblright{} To help was to bring your strength \textbf{toward} somebody. Not to take over, not to fix — to stand beside and add what you have.

English took the same stem twice. \emph{Aid} is the plain one. An \emph{adjutant} is the officer who stands beside a commander and adds capacity.

Said alone — \emph{ayuda} — it is a call. Said with \emph{por favor}, it is a request.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Your first repair word that asks for a person, not a repetition.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la ayuda}
  \item \emph{ayuda, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — ayuda, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{adiutare} mean, literally? (To bring strength toward.) Which English word is it, worn down? (\emph{Aid}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el momento]{el momento — the tilt of a balance}

\label{lesson:ES-C303-momento}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el momento} — \textquotedblleft{}a moment.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{momentum} came from \emph{movere}, \textquotedblleft{}to move,\textquotedblright{} and it did not mean time at all. It meant the \textbf{smallest movement that tips a balance} — the last grain that makes one pan drop.

That is a weight, not a duration. But the tipping happens in an instant, and the word slid from the movement to the instant. English kept the original sense in \emph{momentum} and the borrowed sense in \emph{moment}.

\emph{Un momento, por favor} buys you that instant — and it is the politest thing you can say when you need to think.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two repair words now: one asks for a person, one asks for time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el momento}
  \item \emph{un momento, por favor}
  \item \emph{un momento — no entiendo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{momentum} weigh? (The last grain that tips a balance.) What do you say to buy an instant? (\emph{Un momento, por favor}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[otra vez]{otra vez — another turn round}

\label{lesson:ES-C303-otra-vez}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{otra vez} — \textquotedblleft{}again.\textquotedblright{}

Word by word it is \textquotedblleft{}another turn.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Vez} is Latin \emph{vicem}, and \emph{vicem} meant a \textbf{turn taken in rotation} — your go, coming round again.

English holds that exact word in several places. \emph{Vice versa} is \textquotedblleft{}the turn having been changed.\textquotedblright{} A \emph{vicar} stands in somebody else's turn. A \emph{vice-}president takes the turn of the president.

So \emph{otra vez} does not say \textquotedblleft{}repeat.\textquotedblright{} It says \textbf{another go round} — a kinder thing to ask of a stranger, and it pairs with what you already have.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three ways to repair now — ask for a person, for time, or for another go.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{otra vez}
  \item \emph{otra vez, por favor}
  \item \emph{más despacio, otra vez, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{vez}? (A turn, coming round.) Which English phrase hides the same word? (\emph{Vice versa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[no sé]{no sé — what you have not tasted}

\label{lesson:ES-C303-no-se}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{no sé} — \textquotedblleft{}I do not know.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Sé} comes from Latin \textbf{sapere}, and \emph{sapere} meant \textbf{to taste} — to have flavour, and then to have the discernment that tasting implies.

Follow it into English and the metaphor is still warm. \emph{Savour} is the taste itself. \emph{Insipid} is \emph{in-} plus \emph{sapidus}: without flavour. \emph{Sapient} — and \emph{Homo sapiens} — is \textquotedblleft{}the one that has tasted,\textquotedblright{} a far more modest name for our species than it usually sounds.

So \emph{no sé} is not a failure. It is \textquotedblleft{}I have not tasted that.\textquotedblright{} Note the written mark: \emph{sé} with an accent is \textquotedblleft{}I know\textquotedblright{}; \emph{se} without one is a different word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fourth repair: the honest one, when there is nothing to ask for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{no sé}
  \item \emph{no sé, lo siento}
  \item \emph{no sé — más despacio, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{sapere} mean first? (To taste.) What is \emph{Homo sapiens}, literally? (The one that has tasted.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿qué significa?]{¿qué significa? — asking for the meaning, not the word}

\label{lesson:ES-C303-que-significa}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{¿qué significa?} — \textquotedblleft{}what does it mean?\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Significar} is Latin \emph{significare}, and it takes apart cleanly: \emph{signum}, \textquotedblleft{}a sign,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{facere}, \textquotedblleft{}to make.\textquotedblright{} To mean something was \textbf{to make a sign} of it.

English took the whole family: \emph{sign}, \emph{signal}, \emph{signify}, \emph{significant}, and \emph{design} — \emph{de-} plus \emph{signare}, to mark something out.

This is the twin of the question you cannot ask yet. One asks for a word you do not have; this one asks for the \textbf{meaning} of a word you have just heard and did not follow. Between them they cover both directions, and either one turns a stranger into a source.

Point at the written word, or say it back, and ask.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five repairs, and the last one gets you meanings rather than words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿qué significa?}
  \item \emph{disculpe, ¿qué significa?}
  \item \emph{no entiendo. ¿qué significa?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Take \emph{significare} apart. (\emph{Signum} a sign, \emph{facere} to make.) Which English word is \emph{de-} plus \emph{signare}? (\emph{Design}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
